answers.l: Urban Müller, 1993. Eight commands, designed so its compiler could be only a couple hundred bytes.
Chris Pressey, 1993. Two-dimensional, and designed to be as hard to compile as possible.
Released April 1, 2003. Only spaces, tabs and newlines mean anything.
Programs read like lolcats. HAI opens a program and KTHXBYE ends it.
Ben Olmstead, 1998, named for the eighth circle of hell. The first working program was found two years later by a search algorithm.
Don Woods and James Lyon, 1972. Programs that say PLEASE too rarely, or too often, are rejected.
Programs are plays. Characters are variables, and insults are negative numbers.
Any JavaScript, written with six characters: [ ] ( ) ! +.
David Morgan-Mar. Programs are bitmaps that look like Mondrian paintings.
Also by David Morgan-Mar. Programs are recipes, and ideally the recipe is edible.
Brainf*ck for orangutans. The only words are Ook. Ook? and Ook!
Dylan Beattie, 2018. Programs are power ballads.
Every keyword is a Schwarzenegger line. IT’S SHOWTIME begins the main method.
An object-oriented language written in emoji.
H prints hello world, Q prints the program’s source, 9 sings 99 Bottles of Beer, + increments an accumulator you can never read.
Stack-based and built for code golf.
Brainf*ck, but moo.
David Madore, 1999. Pure combinatory logic with no variables.
Wouter van Oortmerssen, 1993. A stack language with a 1024-byte compiler. It inspired Brainf*ck and Befunge.
John Conway. A program is a list of fractions.
The source code is laid out on a hexagonal grid.
"Fish." A 2D stack language whose instruction pointer swims around the source.
Only brackets and a stack.
A golfing language. The name is hexadecimal for "osable".
A golfing language with its own 256-character code page.
A golfing language that compiles to Python.
Only the length of the program matters. Even small programs are astronomically long.
A program is one symbol repeated. Its count encodes a Brainf*ck program.
Statements run in no particular order, whenever the interpreter feels like it.
John Colagioia’s language of nondeterministic string rewriting.
Four commands and no loops: increment, decrement, square and output.
Programs are MIDI files. Intervals between notes are the syntax.
Programs are nested empty Windows folders, so every source file is zero bytes.
Drive a taxi around a town map to move values. Run out of gas and the program dies.
Chris Barker’s language with a single combinator.
Chris Barker again: every binary string is a valid program.
John Tromp’s encoding of lambda calculus in bits.
Corrado Böhm, 1964. Brainf*ck is essentially P′′ plus input and output.
A stack language whose stack holds programs instead of numbers.
Programs are made of w, W and v, so source code looks like grass.
A program is a length and a random seed that regenerate a Befunge program.
Instructions are London Underground stations, after the radio panel game.
One keyword: chicken.

nope.apl: Not esoteric. Just ahead of its time.
nope.perl: Tempting, but it’s a real language.
nope.haskell: "Avoid success at all costs," maybe, but not esoteric.
nope.regex: Unreadable is not the same as esoteric.
